definitions.text: Some of these can be measured directly and indirectly using some tools and instruments such as length of an object using a ruler, time duration of an event using a clock, the temperature (the degree of hotness) of somebody using a thermometer. They are called physical quantities.
Other quantities quoted above such as love, affection, fear, wisdom, and beauty cannot be measured using tools and instruments. They often pertain to the perception or interpretation of the observer.
Out of these, the scientists have selected arbitrarily some quantities to play a key role. They are called base quantities.
All the quantities which can be described in terms of one or more base quantities are called derived physical quantities.
A measurement is a process of comparison of an unknown quantity with a widely accepted standard quantity.
This standard of measurement is known as a unit.
The units which can be expressed in terms of base units are called derived units.
Prefixes are the words or symbols added before SI unit such as milli, centi, kilo, mega, giga (Table 1.4).
It is short way of representing very large or very small numbers.
Least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument.
If the metre ruler is read from an angle, such as from point A or C, the object will appear to be of different length. This is known as parallax error.
If on joining the jaws A and B, the zeros of the main scale and Vernier scale do not exactly coincide with each other then there is an error in the instrument called zero error.
In any measurement, the accurately known digits and the first doubtful digit are known-as significant figures.

definitions.term: Significant-figure rule for zeros between digits
definitions.text: A zero between two digits is considered significant. For example in 5.06m, the number of significant figures is 3.
Zeros on the left side of the measured value are not significant. For example, in 0.0034 m, the number of significant figures is 2.

definitions.term: Significant-figure rule for zeros after a decimal
definitions.text: Zeros on the right side of a decimal are considered significant. For example, in 2.40 mm the significant digits are 3.
If numbers are recorded in scientific notation, then all the digits before the exponent are significant. For example, in 3.50 × 10⁴m, the significant figures are 3.

To write numbers using scientific notation, move the decimal point until only one non-zero digit remains on the left. Then count the number of places through which the decimal point is moved and use this number as the power or exponents of 10.

When rounding off numbers to a certain number of significant figures, do so to the nearest value. If the last digit is more than 5, the retained digit is increased by one and if it is less than 5, it is retained as such.

formulas.use: State a measured quantity; number is dimensionless and the unit is the relevant unit of that quantity.
Find area from two lengths (length and breadth in m; area in m²).
Find speed from distance and time (speed in m s⁻¹, distance in m, time in s).
Convert one day to seconds (day is a time interval; s is the SI unit of time; k = 10³).
Convert one week to seconds (week and day are time intervals; s is the SI unit of time; k = 10³).
Use the exercise’s 30-day month to convert a month to seconds (month and day are time intervals; s is the SI unit of time; M = 10⁶).
Write a number in scientific notation; x has the unit of the measured quantity, while a and n are dimensionless.

formulas.formula: For addition or subtraction: a × 10ⁿ ± b × 10ⁿ = (a ± b) × 10ⁿ
formulas.use: Add or subtract values after making their powers of 10 equal; the quantities must have the same unit.
Multiply values in scientific notation; the resulting unit is the product of the units of the two quantities.
Divide values in scientific notation; the resulting unit is the numerator unit divided by the denominator unit.

formulas.formula: Least count of Vernier Callipers = 1 main-scale division − 1 Vernier-scale division
formulas.use: Find Vernier Callipers least count (both scale divisions must use the same length unit; least count is in that unit).

formulas.formula: Length = main-scale reading + (least count × Vernier-scale reading)
formulas.use: Find an observed Vernier Callipers length (readings and least count in the same length unit; Vernier-scale reading is a number of divisions).

formulas.formula: Least count of screw gauge = pitch ÷ number of circular-scale divisions
formulas.use: Find micrometer screw gauge least count (pitch and least count in mm or m; number of divisions is dimensionless).

formulas.formula: Thickness = main-scale reading + (circular-scale reading × least count)
formulas.use: Find an observed screw-gauge thickness (main-scale reading and least count in the same length unit; circular-scale reading is a number of divisions).

formulas.formula: Corrected reading = observed reading − zero error (positive zero error); corrected reading = observed reading + zero error (negative zero error)
formulas.use: Correct an instrument reading for zero error (all readings and zero error in the same length unit).

formulas.formula: Volume of solid = final liquid reading − initial liquid reading
formulas.use: Find a solid’s volume by displacement in a measuring cylinder (all volumes in the same unit, such as cm³ or mL).

formulas.formula: 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³
formulas.use: Convert volume units or convert density from g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³ (volume in cm³ or mL; density in the stated units).

fullMarks: For a definition or law, write the complete statement clearly; for a comparison question, name both quantities or units being compared.
In SI-unit questions, write each physical quantity with its correct unit name and symbol; keep symbols in the correct case, such as K, A, m and kg.
For scientific notation, show how the decimal point is moved and use a positive exponent when it moves left and a negative exponent when it moves right.
For addition or subtraction in scientific notation, first make the powers of 10 equal; then combine the coefficients and write the answer in normalized scientific notation.
For instrument numericals, show the scale reading, least count, formula, substitution and final answer with a unit; apply the zero-error correction if the question gives one.
For a metre-scale measurement, avoid parallax by placing the eye directly above the reading; if the zero end is worn, start from a clear mark and subtract that starting reading.
For a displacement measurement, record both initial and final liquid readings and state that the difference is the solid’s volume.
For significant-figure questions, count leading, captive and trailing zeros by the stated rules; keep the required significant figures and unit in the final answer.
mistakes: Writing a number without a unit: include the unit in the final answer because a measurement has both a number and a unit.
Treating leading zeros as significant: zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count, so 0.0045 has two significant figures.
Adding or subtracting scientific-notation values with different exponents directly: first rewrite them with the same power of 10.
Forgetting that the Vernier or circular-scale reading is multiplied by the least count: show the multiplication before adding the main-scale reading.
Using the wrong sign for zero-error correction: subtract a positive zero error and add a negative zero error as instructed for the instrument.
Reading a scale from an angle or reading a water meniscus from above: keep the eye level with the reading and directly in front of the scale.
Using incorrect symbol case or spacing, such as writing K as k or placing a space between a prefix and unit: write symbols correctly and keep a prefix attached to its unit.

shortTheory.question: What is measurement? Name its two parts.
shortTheory.answer: A measurement is a process of comparison of an unknown quantity with a widely accepted standard quantity. A measurement consists of two parts, a number and a unit.

shortTheory.question: Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?
shortTheory.answer: This measurement may result in confusion as the measurement of different people may differ from each other because of different sizes of their hands, arms or steps. To avoid such confusion, there is a need of a standard so that measurement by any person may result the same.

shortTheory.question: Write the name of 3 base quantities and 3 derived quantities.
shortTheory.answer: Base quantities include length, mass and time. Derived quantities include speed, area and volume.

shortTheory.question: Write the name and symbols of all SI base units.
shortTheory.answer: Length — metre (m); mass — kilogram (kg); time — second (s); temperature — kelvin (K); electric current — ampere (A); intensity of light — candela (cd); amount of substance — mole (mol).

shortTheory.question: Why prefix is used? Name three sub-multiple and three multiple prefixes with their symbols.
shortTheory.answer: The use of prefixes makes large and small quantities simple to write down. Three sub-multiple prefixes are milli (m), centi (c) and micro (μ). Three multiple prefixes are kilo (k), mega (M) and giga (G).

shortTheory.question: Can a non-physical quantity be measured? If yes, then how?
shortTheory.answer: Other quantities quoted above such as love, affection, fear, wisdom, and beauty cannot be measured using tools and instruments. They often pertain to the perception or interpretation of the observer. They can be described or qualitatively or compared using some pre-determined criteria, indices or through survey techniques.
